subtopic: Electric Conduction and Conductance of Solutions
stem: The molar conductivity of 0.05 M \(\mathrm{BaCl_2}\) solution at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is 223 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\). What is its conductivity ?
solution:
\(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\,k}{c}\) or \(k = \dfrac{\Lambda c}{1000}\)

\(\Lambda = 223\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\), \(c = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

Hence

\(k = \dfrac{223\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}{1000\ \mathrm{cm^3\ L^{-1}}}\)

\(= 0.01115\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

subtopic: Electric Conduction and Conductance of Solutions
stem: Calculate the molar conductivity of \(\mathrm{AgI}\) at zero concentration if the molar conductivities of \(\mathrm{NaI}\), \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{NaNO_3}\) at zero concentration are respectively, 126.9, 133.4 and 121.5 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
According to Kohrausch law,

i. \(\Lambda_0(\mathrm{NaI}) = \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Na^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{I^\ominus}} = 126.9\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

ii. \(\Lambda_0(\mathrm{AgNO_3}) = \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{NO_3^\ominus}} = 133.4\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

iii. \(\Lambda_0(\mathrm{NaNO_3}) = \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Na^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{NO_3^\ominus}} = 121.5\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

Eq. (i) + eq. (ii) - eq. (iii) gives

\(\Lambda_0(\mathrm{NaI}) + \Lambda_0(\mathrm{AgNO_3}) - \Lambda_0(\mathrm{NaNO_3})\)

\(= \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Na^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{I^\ominus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{NO_3^\ominus}} - \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Na^\oplus}} - \lambda^0_{\mathrm{NO_3^\ominus}}\)

\(= \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{I^\ominus}} = \Lambda_0(\mathrm{AgI})\)

\(= 126.9\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}} + 133.4\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}} - 121.5\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 138.8\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

subtopic: Electric Conduction and Conductance of Solutions
stem: Calculate molar conductivities at zero concentration for \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\). Given : molar ionic conductivitis of \(\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}\), \(\mathrm{Na^\oplus}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) ions are respectively, 104, 76.4, 50.1 and 159.6 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
According to Kohrausch law,

i. \(\Lambda_0(\mathrm{CaCl_2}) = \lambda^0_{\mathrm{Ca^{2\oplus}}} + 2\lambda^0_{\mathrm{Cl^\ominus}}\)

\(= 104\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}} + 2 \times 76.4\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 256.8\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

ii. \(\Lambda_0(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}) = 2\lambda^0_{\mathrm{Na^\oplus}} + \lambda^0_{\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}}\)

\(= 2 \times 50.1\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}} + 159.6\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 259.8\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

subtopic: Electric Conduction and Conductance of Solutions
stem: The molar conductivity of 0.01M acetic acid at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is 16.5 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\). Calculate its degree of dissociation in 0.01 M solution and dissociation constant if molar conductivity of acetic acid at zero concentration is 390.7 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working substitutes \(\Lambda_c = 16.6\) where its own stem states 16.5 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\). The printed result 0.0422 follows from 16.5 (16.5/390.7 = 0.0422, whereas 16.6/390.7 = 0.0425), so the stem and the final answer agree with each other and only the substituted value was wrong. The line has been corrected to 16.5; the answers 0.0422 and \(1.85 \times 10^{-5}\) are unaffected.]

The degree of dissociation,

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_c}{\Lambda_0} = \dfrac{16.5\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}}{390.7\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.0422\)

\(K_a = \dfrac{\alpha^2 c}{1 - \alpha} = \dfrac{(0.0422)^2 \times 0.01}{(1 - 0.0422)} = 1.85 \times 10^{-5}\)

subtopic: Electric Conduction and Conductance of Solutions
stem: A conductivity cell containing 0.01M \(\mathrm{KCl}\) gives at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) the resistance of 604 ohms. The same cell containing 0.001M \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) gives resistance of 6530 ohms. Calculate the molar conductivity of 0.001M \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\). [Conductivity of 0.01M \(\mathrm{KCl}\) at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is 0.00141 \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)]
solution:
i. Calculation of cell constant

Cell constant \(= k_{\mathrm{KCl}} \times R_{\mathrm{KCl}}\)

\(= 0.00141\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} \times 604\ \Omega = 0.852\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

ii. Calculation of conductiviy of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\),

\(k = \dfrac{\text{Cell constant}}{R}\) where \(R = 6530\ \Omega\)

\(= \dfrac{0.852\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{6530\ \Omega} = 1.3 \times 10^{-4}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

iii. Calculation of molar conductivity of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\)

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\,k}{c}\) where \(c = 0.001\ \mathrm{M}\)

\(= \dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{cm^3\ L^{-1}} \times 1.3 \times 10^{-4}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{0.001\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}\)

\(= 130\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem: What is the mass of \(\mathrm{Cu}\) metal produced at the cathode during the passage of 5 ampere current through \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) solution for 100 minutes. Molar mass of \(\mathrm{Cu}\) is 63.5 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
i. Stoichiometry for the formation of \(\mathrm{Cu}\) is

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\,\mathrm{e^\ominus} = \mathrm{Cu(s)}\)

Hence, mole ratio \(= \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}}\)

ii. Mass of \(\mathrm{Cu}\) formed,

\(W = \dfrac{I\ (\mathrm{A}) \times t\ (\mathrm{s})}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})} \times \text{mole ratio} \times \text{molar mass of Cu}\)

\(= \dfrac{5\ \mathrm{A} \times 100 \times 60\ \mathrm{s}}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})} \times \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^-}} \times 63.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 9.87\ \mathrm{g}\)

stem: How long will it take to produce 2.415 g of \(\mathrm{Ag}\) metal from its salt solution by passing a current of 3 ampere ? Molar mass of \(\mathrm{Ag}\) is 107.9 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
i. Stoichiometry :

\(\mathrm{Ag^\oplus(aq)} + \mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag(s)}\)

mole ratio \(= \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{1\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}}\)

ii. \(W = \dfrac{I\ (\mathrm{A}) \times t\ (\mathrm{s})}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})} \times \text{mole ratio} \times \text{molar mass of Ag}\)

\(2.415\ \mathrm{g} = \dfrac{3\ \mathrm{A} \times t}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})} \times \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{1\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}} \times 107.9\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(t = \dfrac{2.415 \times 96500\ (\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{A\,s})}{3\ \mathrm{A} \times 107.9}\)

\(= 720\ \mathrm{s} = 12\) min.

stem: How many moles of electrons are required for reduction of 3 moles of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) to \(\mathrm{Zn}\) ? How many Faradays of electricity will be required ?
solution:
i. The balanced equation for the reduction of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) to \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is

\(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn(s)}\)

The equation shows that 1 mole of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Zn}\) by 2 moles of electrons. For reduction of 3 moles of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) 6 moles of electrons will be required.

**Faraday (96500 Coulombs) is the amount of charge on one mole of electrons**. Therefore, for 6 moles of electrons, 6 F electricity will be required.

stem: In a certain electrolysis experiment 4.36 g of \(\mathrm{Zn}\) are deposited in one cell containing \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) solution. Calculate the mass of \(\mathrm{Al}\) deposited in another cell containing \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) solution connected in series with \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4}\) cell. Molar masses of \(\mathrm{Zn}\) and \(\mathrm{Al}\) are 65.4 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) and 27 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), respectively.
solution:
Cell 1 :

\(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn(s)}\)

\((\text{mole ratio})_1 = \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}}\)

Cell 2 :

\(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Al(s)}\)

\((\text{mole ratio})_2 = \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{3\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}}\)

\(\dfrac{W_1}{(\text{mole ratio})_1 \times M_1} = \dfrac{W_2}{(\text{mole ratio})_2 \times M_2}\)

\(W_1 = 4.36\ \mathrm{g}\), \(M_1 = 65.4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), \(M_2 = 27\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

Substitution of the quantities gives

\(\dfrac{4.36\ \mathrm{g}}{1\ \mathrm{mol}/2\ \mathrm{mol\ e} \times 65.4\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = \dfrac{W_2}{1\ \mathrm{mol}/3\ \mathrm{mol\ e^-} \times 27\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}}\)

or \(\dfrac{4.36\ \mathrm{g} \times 2}{65.4} = \dfrac{W_2 \times 3}{27}\)

Hence, \(W_2 = \dfrac{4.36\ \mathrm{g} \times 2 \times 27}{65.4 \times 3} = 1.2\ \mathrm{g}\)

stem: Calculate the voltage of the cell, \(\mathrm{Sn(s)}\,|\,\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\,(0.02\mathrm{M})\,||\,\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}\,(0.01\mathrm{M})\,|\,\mathrm{Ag(s)}\) at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\). \(E^0_{Sn} = -0.136\) V, \(E^0_{Ag} = 0.800\) V.
solution:
First we write the cell reaction.

\(\mathrm{Sn(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\,(0.02\mathrm{M}) + 2\,\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)  (oxidation at anode)

\([\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}\,(0.01\mathrm{M}) + \mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag(s)}] \times 2\)  (reduction at cathode)

\(\mathrm{Sn(s)} + 2\,\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}\,(0.01\mathrm{M}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\,(0.02\ \mathrm{M}) + 2\,\mathrm{Ag(s)}\)  (overall cell reaction)

The cell potential is given by

\(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}]^2}\)

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{Ag} - E^0_{Sn} = 0.8\ \mathrm{V} + 0.136\ \mathrm{V} = 0.936\ \mathrm{V}\)

Hence,

\(E_{cell} = 0.936\,\mathrm{V} - \dfrac{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}\dfrac{0.02}{(0.01)^2}\)

\(= 0.936\,\mathrm{V} - \dfrac{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10} 200\)

\(= 0.936\,\mathrm{V} - \dfrac{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}}{2} \times 2.301\)

\(= 0.936\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0681\,\mathrm{V} = 0.8679\ \mathrm{V}\)

stem: The standard potential of the electrode, \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\,(0.02\ \mathrm{M})\,|\,\mathrm{Zn(s)}\) is \(-0.76\) V. Calculate its potential.
solution:
[Textbook note (not an error): the stem calls \(-0.76\) V the "standard potential of the electrode \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\,(0.02\ \mathrm{M})\,|\,\mathrm{Zn(s)}\)", but a standard potential is by definition the value at 1 M. What is meant is that the standard potential of the \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\,|\,\mathrm{Zn}\) electrode is \(-0.76\) V and this particular electrode is operating at 0.02 M — which is exactly how the printed solution uses the two numbers. The working and the answer are correct as printed.]

Electrode reaction :

\(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\,(0.02\mathrm{M}) + 2\,\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn(s)}\)

\(E_{Zn} = E^0_{Zn} - \dfrac{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}}{n}\log_{10}\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}]}\)

\(= -0.76\ \mathrm{V} + \dfrac{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}(0.02)\)

\(= -0.76\ \mathrm{V} + \dfrac{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}}{2} \times (-1.6990)\)

\(= -0.76\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0503\,\mathrm{V} = -0.81\ \mathrm{V}\)

stem:
Calculate standard Gibbs energy change and equilibrium constant at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) for the cell reaction,

\(\mathrm{Cd(s)} + \mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{Sn(s)}\)

Given : \(E^0_{Cd} = -0.403\) V and \(E^0_{Sn} = -0.136\) V. Write formula of the cell.
solution:
i. The cell is made of two electrodes, \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Cd(s)}\) and \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Sn(s)}\). \(E^0\) value for \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Sn(s)}\) electrode is higher than that of \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Cd(s)}\) electrode. Hence, \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Sn(s)}\) electrode is cathode and \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Cd(s)}\) anode. Cell formula is \(\mathrm{Cd(s)}\,|\,\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,||\,\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}(aq)}\,|\,\mathrm{Sn(s)}\)

ii. \(\Delta G^0 = -n\mathrm{F}E^0_{cell}\)

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{Sn} - E^0_{Cd} = -0.136\ \mathrm{V} - (-0.403\ \mathrm{V}) = 0.267\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(n = 2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}\)

\(\Delta G^0 = -2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus} \times 96500\ \mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus} \times 0.267\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(= -51531\ \mathrm{V\,C} = -51531\ \mathrm{J} = -51.53\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

iii. \(E^0_{cell} = \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}K\)

\(0.267\ \mathrm{V} = \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}K\)

\(\log_{10}K = \dfrac{0.267 \times 2}{0.0592} = 9.0203\)

\(K = \text{antilog } 9.0203 = 1.05 \times 10^{9}\)
